4/4/2024 Spanky Training/Handling Tips:? Drop off enrichment to help him expend some mental energy if possible before taking him out. (Frozen enrichment can be found in the white freezer located in the back sally port)? Before opening the kennel, show him your treats and ask him to “sit” and then give him a treat when he sits. If he’s excited, it  may take a few asks before he responds. Then use the treat on the other side of the loop trick to get the leash on him.? Keep treats visible as you walk and throw them on the ground for him to “find it” until you get outside or he shifts his attention to his surroundings ? If he bites at the leash, continue walking while ignoring the behavior. If you are in a contained area, intersperse dropping the leash in response to any increase in tugging. As soon as there is a slight pause or decrease in intensity, redirect him with “down” and/or “sit” and then give him a treat with verbal praise. Repeat as needed.? Start walking again, a treat + praise or throwing treat for him to "find it" every few steps ? If he starts to bite again, correct him by saying “eh” and then reset his behavior with “down” or “sit” followed by treat + praise. Then resume walking ? Once biting stops, keep him engaged and reinforce good walking with intermittent treats thrown for him to find? When un/re-leashing, first ask him to “sit” first and then give him a treat.  ** If you try to pull the leash away from him, he will tug back. If you ignore, drop the leash (he's not a runner), and redirect him with a command, then he will drop the leash to fetch the treat! ** Continue asking him to "find it" until he is leading the walk and no longer looking at you. At this point, he'll be easy on leash ** Any time you need to adjust/tighten/handle the leash, ask him to do something and reward him right as you do it (this results in him focusing on what you want him to do vs. the leash you're adjusting)

It was fun being out with him and seeing him so much more at ease outside of the shelter! Observing his behavior out of the shelter has me even more confident that being in a home where he can decompress and has regular interaction and stimulation will do wonders at eliminating any OA and leash biting!
